messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Javier, a 53-year-old Latin American man who worked as a tax consultant, came to treatment after more than a year of living as if the world had become a place he could not fully read. He described a life that had once been structured and predictable: days spent at his desk with clients’ returns, evenings alone since his divorce, and the familiar rhythm of commuting to and from his office. That changed after an encounter with police that he experienced as violent and humiliating. He did not describe the event in abstract terms; he returned repeatedly to the details that stayed with him. The officers had approached him suddenly, and in the confusion he was injured. What remained most vivid was the sight of wounds and bruises afterward, both on himself and on other victims he later saw in his mind when he tried to sleep. From that day on, injuries had a startling power over him. If he saw someone with a cut on their face, blood on a sleeve, or a bandaged hand in a waiting room, he felt pulled back to the scene, as if the injury itself carried him directly into the moment when he had felt powerless and exposed.

In the months after the incident, Javier began to notice that the smallest reminders could pull him into the same unsettled state. A client mentioning an arrest, a news image of a person being restrained, or even his own bodily discomfort could leave him tense and distracted. He spoke especially about pain in a part of his body that had been hurt during the encounter; when that area ached, he was no longer simply aware of discomfort but was flooded with the sense that something bad was again about to happen. He would sit rigidly, waiting for the feeling to pass, and he found it hard to trust that the sensation was only physical. At work, this made even ordinary days feel precarious. As a tax consultant, he often met clients in unfamiliar offices or visited new buildings for appointments, and he noticed that he could not settle unless he first found the exits. He would scan hallways, ask himself how he would get out quickly, and identify an escape route before he could focus on the meeting. If a client changed the location at the last minute, he became visibly uneasy. He also began to avoid unfamiliar places whenever he could, explaining to himself that he simply could not assess the danger there. He preferred routes and rooms he already knew, not because he was looking for comfort in any sentimental sense, but because unfamiliar settings left him feeling vulnerable in a way he could not easily dismiss.

Over time, Javier’s vigilance spread into ordinary movement through the day. Walking to his car after work, sitting in a restaurant, or standing in line at a store, he frequently looked behind him to check whether someone was following him. He did this almost automatically, with a quick turn of the head that left him embarrassed when he noticed others watching. He was certain that if he did not keep checking, he would miss the moment when danger appeared. This habit narrowed his life in quiet ways. He stopped lingering after meetings, declined invitations to places he had not been before, and organized his schedule around routes and environments he could already picture in his mind. His divorce had already left him living alone, and the distance he felt from others deepened as he began to assume that no one around him could really understand what had happened. He described himself as isolated and set apart, as if the event had placed him on one side of a line that others could not cross. Even when friends or relatives reached out, he often pulled back, partly because he did not want to explain himself and partly because he felt changed in a way that made ordinary company feel difficult.

As he spoke, Javier returned again and again to a harsh belief that had settled over him: that there was something about him that made the event happen. He did not present this as a passing thought but as a judgment he had carried since the encounter, one that colored how he understood his injuries, his caution, and his loneliness. On difficult days, especially when the pain in his body flared or when he found himself on an unfamiliar street, the thought of whether his life was worth living at all came into view. He did not describe a plan, but he did say that he was no longer sure his life was worth living anymore, and that frightened him. What brought him to seek help was the sense that his world had become smaller and more guarded than he could tolerate, and that he was living from one moment of checking to the next, always bracing for what might come. He hoped treatment might help him feel less trapped in constant alertness and less alone with what happened, though what he feared most was that he would never again be able to move through the world without feeling that he had to watch behind him and find the nearest way out.
